newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi says government being undermined.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi says government being undermined.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi returned home from a European summit in Dublin on Sunday to face dissatisfaction over his coalition's programme and what he called an attempt to undermine his government.

Responding to criticism from industrialists over economic policies, Prodi was quoted in Italian newspapers on Sunday as saying: "In these past days, they have tried to give one last big push to the government, but we will resist".

However Massimo D'Alema, leader of the former communist Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) which is the biggest party in Prodi's centre-left coalition, openly stated his frustrations in an interview in Saturday's La Repubblica newspaper.

D'Alema, while reiterating his full support for the government, said he was dissatisfied with the Olive Tree coalition's lack of action to implement its grand plan to renew and change Italian society and its institutions.

He asked Prodi to "depend more on the PDS" and suggested opening discussions on closer ties with the hard-left Communist Refoundation, which is not part of the coalition but on whose support Prodi relies in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house).
Prodi, when asked to comment on D'Alema's remarks by Italian journalists in Dublin on Saturday, pointed to the fact that nine of his 20 ministers were PDS members.
"This team playing has been undervalued," Prodi said.
D'Alema was quoted in newspapers on Sunday as saying he was not criticising the government, but merely trying to spur it into action.
D'Alema was not the only Prodi ally who said the time had come for a re-assessment of the government's programme.
Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini, who was with Prodi in Dublin, told reporters there on Saturday that the parties in the coalition should meet to discuss future policy.
"It is right that after seven or eight months in government we draw up the policies (we) must follow in 1997," said Dini, who is head of the small Italian Renewal party.
He added that he did not see any need for talks over the actual make-up of Prodi's government, which took office in May.
The Communist Refoundation, which has a party congress in Rome this weekend, rejected outright D'Alema's overtures for fresh discussions with the government.
Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti said he would not make any agreements with the government on future programmes.
"It would be suicide," Bertinotti said. "The PDS and the Refoundation have two very different programmes."
Prodi has devoted much of his time in office to formulating a 1997 budget which he hopes will bring Italy into line with tough criteria for entry into a single European currency.
His government faces three votes of confidence in the Senate on Monday over the budget which it called in order to sweep aside some 3,000 opposition amendments.
Prodi has a comfortable majority in the Senate and his expected victory will strip away the blocking amendments.
Both houses must approve the budget, designed to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) from next year's deficit, by December 31. Costly provisional measures take effect if the deadline is missed.
